diagnostic_evidence.quote: A map $A_\omega \colon \Omega \times \Omega \to \Omega$ is called a binary average

issues.failure_explanation: The claim asserts the argmin defines a map $\Omega\times\Omega\to\Omega$ that is continuous in $\omega$ for every metric space (every metric is continuous, so the stated proviso is vacuous). In general the minimizer need not exist (e.g. $\Omega=\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$, $x=-1,y=1,\omega=1/2$) nor be unique (antipodal points on a sphere), so the Fréchet 'mean' is not a well-defined map and continuity in $\omega$ can fail. Only boundedness follows from the variational characterization.

failure_location.quote: It is easy to verify that if the metric $d$ is continuous as a function of its arguments, then the binary Fr\'echet mean satisfies all the requirements of Definition~\ref{def:average}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the claim to spaces where the binary Fréchet minimizer exists uniquely and depends continuously on $\omega$ (e.g. Hadamard/CAT(0) spaces or small geodesic balls).
issues.overall_effect: The motivating example is false as stated; nothing later depends on it.
issues.title: Binary Fréchet mean claimed to be an average in every metric space
issues.why_classification: Purely an illustrative example; adding the standard existence/uniqueness proviso restores it with no effect on the theory.

issues.failure_explanation: By (4.2) only $t^{k+1}_{2j},t^{k+1}_{2j+1}\in[t^k_j,t^k_{j+1})$, while $t^{k+1}_{2j+2}\in[t^k_{j+1},t^k_{j+2})$; for the dual parameterization $t^{k+1}_{2j+2}>t^k_{j+1}$, so the claimed inclusion fails and for $t\in[t^k_{j+1},t^{k+1}_{2j+2})$ the interpolant $\mathcal{PA}(Q^k;t)$ is an average of $p^k_{j+1},p^k_{j+2}$, whose distance to $p^k_j$ is only bounded by $2\delta(S^k\mathcal P)$, not $\delta(S^k\mathcal P)$ as in (4.10).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the bound (4.10) by $2\delta(S^k\mathcal P)$ (triangle inequality through $p^k_{j+1}$) and adjust the constant $C_S+3$ to $C_S+4$.
issues.overall_effect: The constant in the Cauchy estimate is wrong; the geometric decay and the convergence conclusion are unaffected.
issues.title: False interval inclusion in the third-term bound of the convergence proof
issues.why_classification: A one-line local fix of a constant; the theorem, rate and scope all survive.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The conclusion is that under the condition $\delta (\PP) \le \nu$, the subdivision scheme $W$ has a contractivity factor $\muW$ with a contractivity number $L$.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof only establishes $\delta(W^{kL}\mathcal P)\le\mu_W^k\delta(\mathcal P)$ for $\delta(\mathcal P)\le\nu$. To invoke Theorem convergence one needs a $W$-invariant set on which $W$ is contractive, i.e. $\mathcal D'=\{\mathcal P\in\mathcal D:\delta(\mathcal P)\le\nu\}$ must satisfy $W(\mathcal D')\subset\mathcal D'$; nothing bounds $\delta(W^r\mathcal P)$ for $0<r<L$ (D-S controls only even points). Counterexample in $\mathbb R$: $S$ = elementary scheme declared with $L=2,\mu=1/4$; $W$ acting on 'smooth' data ($|\Delta p_j|\le1$) by $W(\mathcal P)_{2j}=p_j$, $W(\mathcal P)_{2j+1}=\tfrac12(p_j+p_{j+1})+K$ ($K=10$) and on the resulting zigzag data by undoing the shift so that $W^2=S^2$ exactly on smooth data. With $\mathcal D$ = smooth ∪ zigzag data, $W$ is local, D-S ($C_W=2$), maps $\mathcal D$ to itself, $W^2$ is in first-type proximity to $S^2$ ($C=1,\varepsilon=1$), yet from smooth data with tiny $\delta$ the odd levels have amplitude-$K$ spikes and $W$ does not converge, contradicting the statement.

failure_location.quote: Finally, the weak convergence of the scheme $W$ follows by Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence} since $W$ has a contractivity factor when $\delta(\PP)$ is small enough, it is D-S in $\D$, and it maps $\D$ onto itself.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a hypothesis controlling intermediate steps, e.g. a one-step growth bound $\delta(W(\mathcal P))\le C'\delta(\mathcal P)$ on $\mathcal D$ (then shrink the threshold (5.3) accordingly), or restrict the statement to $L=1$.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem main_proximity is false as stated for contractivity number $L>1$; the case $L=1$ (used in Corollary cor:added-1) is unaffected.
issues.title: First-type proximity theorem: contractivity on the subsequence $kL$ does not give an invariant set for Theorem convergence when $L>1$
issues.why_classification: A genuine counterexample exists, so the statement must be weakened by an extra hypothesis or a smaller threshold; a comparable result and the paper's application survive without new architecture.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In addition, the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence_proximity_2ndType} does not rely on a contractivity factor of $S_1$ and so we do not require $S_1$ to have the D-S property.
Thus, the rest of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence_proximity_2ndType} is valid for

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem's hypotheses (same parameterization, invariance of $\mathcal D$, order-0 proximity) contain no displacement-safe condition, yet the proof bounds the middle term by $C_{S_1}\delta(S_1^\ell\mathcal P)$ 'since $S_1$ is D-S', and the remark explicitly denies the need for D-S. The hypothesis is necessary: take $S_1=S_2$ = Chaikin's scheme plus a fixed translation $e\neq0$ at every new point. $S_2$ is contractive ($\mu=1/2,L=1$), proximity holds with distance $0$, but the interpolants $f^k$ are translated by $e$ at each level and never converge.

failure_location.quote: The middle term on the RHS of~\eqref{eqn:W_proof_main} is bounded by $C_{S_1} \delta (S_1^{\ell} (\PP))$ since $S_1$ is D-S.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add 'S_1 is displacement-safe in $\mathcal D$' to the hypotheses of Theorems convergence_proximity_2ndType and C1_m1 and delete the claim in Remark rem:prox_2 that D-S is not required.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem convergence_proximity_2ndType is false as stated; Theorem C1_m1 inherits the gap through its appeal to this theorem and its proof. The application (Theorem C1_manifold) uses a D-S scheme and survives.
issues.title: Second-type convergence theorem uses D-S of $S_1$, which is not assumed and is necessary
issues.why_classification: The stated theorem is false and an advertised feature (no D-S needed) is withdrawn, but adding the hypothesis the proof already uses restores a comparable result.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: In particular, note that the power of $\eta$ scales like $\cdot/L$ with respect to the number of refinements.

issues.failure_explanation: Proximity of $S_1^{L}$ to $S_2^{L}$ is indexed by $\mathcal P^j=S_1^{jL}\mathcal P$, so after $\ell$ refinements the bound is $E\eta^{\ell/L+1}$ (and only for $L\mid\ell$; other residues require applying the definition to $S_1^r\mathcal P$). The proofs of both second-type theorems use $\eta^{\ell-L+1}$ instead. In Theorem convergence_proximity_2ndType this is harmless (the correct exponent still yields $\alpha^{\lfloor\ell/L\rfloor}$ decay). In Theorem C1_m1 it is fatal for $L_1>1$: the divided-difference error is $2^\ell E\eta^{\ell/L_1+1}$, which tends to zero only if $\eta<2^{-L_1}$, whereas order 1 only requires $\eta<1/2$. Counterexample with $L_1=2$: $S_2$ = Chaikin in $\mathbb R^2$ (satisfies (6.4) with $L_1=2,\mu_1=1/4$), $S_1$ = Chaikin on the $x$-coordinate and Chaikin plus an alternating-sign perturbation $\pm c|\Delta x_j|^{0.6}$ on the $y$-coordinate: $S_1^2$ is in order-1 proximity to $S_2^2$ with $\eta=2^{-1.2}<1/2$, all other hypotheses hold, but the $y$-limit is a Weierstrass-type Hölder-0.6 function, not $C^1$.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Require $\eta<2^{-L_1}$ in Theorem C1_m1 (or define the order relative to the number of single refinements), rewrite the exponents in (6.3) and the divided-difference bound as $\eta^{\lfloor\ell/L\rfloor}$, and handle residues $\ell\not\equiv0\ (\mathrm{mod}\ L)$ by applying proximity to $S_1^r\mathcal P$ with $E=\max_r E(S_1^r\mathcal P)$.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem C1_m1 is false as stated whenever $L_1>1$; the $L_1=1$ case (used in Lemma lem:added-1 with $\eta=1/4$) survives. The recursion (6.3) in the order-0 theorem also needs the corrected exponent and the shifted-start argument.
issues.title: Exponent of $\eta$ miscounted: order-1 proximity of $S_1^{L_1}$ to $S_2^{L_1}$ gives $2^\ell\eta^{\ell/L_1}$, not $(2\eta)^\ell$
issues.why_classification: The $C^1$ statement is false in an advertised regime ($L_1>1$) and must be weakened by a stronger threshold on $\eta$; the corrected statement and the application remain.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $S_2$ be a subdivision scheme defined on $\R^n$ that satisfies~\eqref{eqn:contractivity_diff} with a contractivity factor $\mudelta$ and a contractivity number $L_1$ in $\D \subset \big( \R^n \big)^\Z$.
Thus, the rest of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence_proximity_2ndType} is valid for

issues.failure_explanation: The statement assumes only first-order contractivity (6.4) of $S_2$, but the proof (i) applies Theorem convergence_proximity_2ndType, which requires zero-order contractivity of $S_2$, asserting 'since $S_2$ is contractive' without hypothesis; and (ii) claims the Cauchy argument of that theorem transfers verbatim to the divided-difference sequences $Q^\ell=\{(t^\ell_j,(\Delta S_1^\ell\mathcal P/2^{-\ell})_j)\}$. That argument's middle term needs a displacement bound for divided differences, $\|(\Delta S_1^{\ell+1}\mathcal P/2^{-\ell-1})_{2j}-(\Delta S_1^{\ell}\mathcal P/2^{-\ell})_j\|\le C\,\delta(\Delta S_1^\ell\mathcal P/2^{-\ell})$, which is a first-order D-S property of a nonlinear scheme, not implied by zero-order D-S, by (6.4), or by the proximity assumption, and it is never established.

failure_location.quote: Moreover, the convergence of $S_1$ is guaranteed by Theorem~\ref{thm:convergence_proximity_2ndType} since $S_2$ is contractive and proximity of order $m=1$ implies proximity of order $m=0$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add to Theorem C1_m1 the hypotheses that $S_2$ is (zero-order) contractive in $\mathcal D$ and that a first-order displacement-safe bound holds for the divided differences (of $S_2$, transferred to $S_1$ via proximity, or directly of $S_1$), and verify these in Lemma lem:added-1.
issues.overall_effect: The $C^1$ theorem rests on unstated hypotheses; even after fixing ISSUE-004/005 the proof of convergence of the divided-difference interpolants is incomplete for general nonlinear $S_1,S_2$. The application to (6.8) (linear $S_2$, where first-order D-S is automatic) is not endangered.
issues.title: Theorem C1_m1 invokes zero-order contractivity of $S_2$ and a first-order displacement bound that are neither assumed nor proved
issues.why_classification: A contained addition of hypotheses (automatic for linear $S_2$) closes the gap and keeps the result and its application; no new global architecture is needed but the omission is a real hole in a main theorem.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $\Omega \subset \R^n$ be a complete Riemannian manifold and let $\D \subseteq \Omega^\Z$.

issues.failure_explanation: The cited estimate from Wallner–Dyn holds for points in a compact region (constant depending on bounds of the second fundamental form). For a complete embedded manifold with unbounded curvature, e.g. the curve $\{(s,\sin s^2)\}\subset\mathbb R^2$, the deviation of the arc-length midpoint from the chord midpoint is $\approx\kappa(s)\|p_0-p_1\|^2/8$ with $\kappa(s)\to\infty$, so no point-independent $C$ exists. Lemma lem:added-1 uses this uniform $C$ to produce a single $E$ valid for all $i\in\mathbb Z$, which fails for unbounded data sequences in such manifolds.
